items.title: Nairobi’s EL Niño flood response faces equity test as drainage works leave informal settlements exposed
items.description: Nairobi’s preparations for the October–December 2026 rainy season are exposing a wider challenge in the city’s flood management: drainage improvements may
content: Nairobi’s preparations for the October–December 2026 rainy season are exposing a wider challenge in the city’s flood management: drainage improvements may reduce surface water accumulation on major roads, but they cannot adequately protect residents living in flood-prone informal settlements without changes to land-use planning, housing policy and community-level disaster preparedness.

The Nairobi City County Governmen t has identified 227 flood-prone hotspots across the capital and launched a multi-agency response involving drainage clearance, river rehabilitation, emergency coordination and planned shelters. The preparations follow Kenya’s August 2026 seasonal forecast, which projected above-average rainfall across approximately 80% of the country during the October–December short rains, with prolonged wet spells and occasional isolated storms.

The county’s response includes drainage and flood-mitigation projects, with reported allocations of KSh2.4 billion, including KSh2 billion for drainage improvements along 19 flood-prone roads. Governor Johnson Sakaja has also said that 26 of 61 critical drainage sites had been cleared as the city prepared for the rainy season. The county has worked with agencies including the Kenya Red Cross, Kenya Urban Roads Authority, Kenya National Highways Authority and Nairobi Rivers Commission.

These measures address an important part of Nairobi’s flood exposure. Blocked drains, accumulated waste, inadequate stormwater infrastructure and restricted river channels can increase the speed and severity of flooding during heavy rainfall. However, research published by the World Resources Institute (WRI) in July 2026 argues that the city’s recurring flood crisis is also shaped by settlement patterns, the loss of natural drainage systems, weak enforcement of land-use regulations and fragmented institutional responsibility.

The distinction is significant because Nairobi’s flood risk is not distributed evenly across the city. Major roads and commercial corridors are important to the movement of people and goods, but residents of informal settlements along the Nairobi, Mathare and Ngong rivers face a different level of exposure. In places such as Mathare, Mukuru, Kayole and parts of Kahawa West, flooding can destroy homes, contaminate water supplies and interrupt the informal economic activities on which households depend.

The WRI report, Flooding in Nairobi’s Informal Settlements: Advancing Equitable and Resilient Solutions , examined the March–May 2024 floods through geospatial analysis, flood modelling, policy research and household surveys in Kibera, Mukuru Viwandani and Mathare. It found that nearly 21,000 families were displaced during the 2024 floods, while more than 147,000 cases of waterborne disease were reported. The flooding also damaged roads, bridges, homes and community infrastructure.

The report identifies a combination of physical and institutional factors that intensify the effects of heavy rainfall. Nairobi’s west-to-east slope and river network influence how water moves through the city, while compacted soils, expanding built-up surfaces and the loss of wetlands and riparian vegetation reduce the landscape’s capacity to absorb and manage runoff. Settlement in floodplains and river corridors further increases the number of people and assets exposed to rising water.

Urban expansion has intensified these pressures. A University of Nairobi study examining land-use changes between 1988 and 2010 found that built-up areas and open land increased by approximately 438%, while agricultural and riparian vegetation declined by about 96%. The findings illustrate how development has altered the city’s natural drainage and water-retention systems over time.

Population growth has also increased pressure on available land and housing. Nairobi’s population rose from approximately 350,000 at independence to nearly 4.4 million in the 2019 census. Informal settlements account for a substantial share of the city’s residents while occupying a relatively small proportion of its land. The Kenya Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis estimates that approximately 60% of Nairobi’s population lives in informal settlements, which occupy about 6% of the county’s land.

For many households, settlement in flood-prone areas is linked to affordability and proximity to employment rather than a lack of awareness about environmental risks. More than 90% of residents in some informal settlements are tenants, meaning they often have limited control over housing quality, land-use decisions or the structural safety of buildings. Moving to safer locations can also mean losing access to casual employment, markets, transport connections and social support networks.

The consequences of flooding therefore extend beyond property damage. The WRI research documents disruptions to sanitation, health services, education and household livelihoods. Flooded pit latrines and contaminated water increase the risk of waterborne illnesses, while traders and small businesses can lose stock and working capital. Children may miss school when pathways and facilities become inaccessible, and women and children face additional protection risks when displacement forces families into temporary shelters.

The effects are particularly difficult to reverse for households with limited savings or access to insurance. A family that loses a home, business inventory or essential documents may take months to recover, even after floodwaters have receded. These costs are not necessarily captured by conventional county progress indicators, which tend to focus on drainage works, cleared channels, infrastructure repairs and the number of identified hotspots.

The March 2026 floods again demonstrated the scale of the city’s exposure. Data compiled by the Copernicus Emergency Management Service, citing Kenya’s Ministry of Interior, recorded 37 flood-related deaths in the Nairobi region between 1 and 24 March. The wider national emergency affected several counties, illustrating the difficulty of managing extreme rainfall through infrastructure interventions alone.

The current response raises questions about how the county measures preparedness and distributes resources. Drainage improvements can reduce immediate hazards, but they do not address the underlying reasons why households continue to live in locations exposed to repeated flooding. Nor do they guarantee that residents will have safe accommodation, accessible evacuation routes or financial support when warnings are issued.

The WRI report recommends a broader approach that combines infrastructure investment with rights-based relocation, restoration of wetlands and riparian corridors, green-grey infrastructure, improved early-warning systems and stronger community participation. These interventions would require coordination between county and national authorities, utility providers, humanitarian organisations and residents.

One priority is to establish social indicators alongside infrastructure targets. Tracking displacement, waterborne disease, school attendance, livelihood losses and access to emergency shelters would provide a clearer picture of how flooding affects households and whether public interventions are reducing vulnerability.

Anticipatory financing could also help households prepare before heavy rainfall reaches critical levels. Cash transfers and other forms of targeted support, activated through reliable weather warnings, could enable vulnerable families to secure essential supplies, protect assets or temporarily relocate. Such measures would need transparent eligibility criteria and coordination with existing social protection programmes.

Relocation and river rehabilitation present another policy challenge. Removing structures from riparian land may reduce exposure, but evictions without affordable alternative housing can push families into other unsafe locations or lead them back to the same flood-prone areas. Resettlement plans therefore need to account for housing costs, employment access, sanitation and the needs of tenants as well as property owners.

Upgrading informal settlements in place, where technically and environmentally feasible, could also reduce risk. Improved stormwater drainage, sanitation, solid-waste collection and accessible evacuation routes would help address immediate vulnerabilities while longer-term land-use planning protects river corridors and natural drainage systems.

Community participation is central to these measures. Residents often have detailed knowledge of local flood patterns, blocked drainage points, evacuation routes and households requiring assistance. Linking community disaster committees to ward-level planning and developing early-warning communication through mobile alerts, community radio and local health networks could improve the speed and reach of emergency responses.

Nairobi’s preparations for the 2026 short rains represent a more coordinated effort than a response focused solely on emergency rescue and recovery. However, the effectiveness of the programme will depend on whether the city can connect infrastructure investment with housing, public health, social protection and land-use policy.

The challenge is not simply to move rainwater away from roads. It is to reduce the number of people forced to live in places where flooding repeatedly threatens their homes, health and livelihoods. As the rainy season progresses, the measure of Nairobi’s preparedness will be whether vulnerable communities can remain safe and recover more quickly, not only whether major roads reopen after the water recedes.

The author is a Sustainability Analyst at Impact Africa Consulting Limited. She holds transboundary knowledge and expertise in ESG strategy, sustainable finance, and impact-driven consulting. She works with organizations to integrate environmental, social, and governance principles into strategy, investment decision-making, and reporting frameworks that support long-term value creation. She writes and speaks on sustainability, development in Africa, and the intersection of finance, impact, and systems change

items.title: US consortium wins huge Kenya mining deal, beating Chinese rivals
items.description: The Mrima Hill site is estimated to hold deposits of critical minerals worth more than $60bn (£45bn).
content: A US-led consortium, Frontier Minerals, has won the tender to develop Kenya's Mrima Hill mining project, beating seven bidders, including companies from China and Australia.
The site is estimated to hold deposits of critical minerals worth more than $60bn (£45bn), including niobium, used in electric vehicles, aerospace and defence technology.
Frontier Minerals says its proposal aims to keep more of the economic benefits in Kenya through "processing and refining of minerals in-country".
The deal comes as Washington seeks greater access to Africa's minerals, aiming to strengthen US supply chains and compete with China.

Frontier Minerals brings together three US companies - Bunker Hill Mining Corp, American Resources Corporation and ReElement Technologies Corporation. The consortium combines expertise in mineral resource development, critical materials supply chains and advanced refining technologies.

A central part of its proposal is to develop mineral processing and refining capacity in Kenya. Brad Barnett from Frontier Minerals said the company wanted the country to capture more value from its mineral resources.
Mrima Hill is located in Kwale County, near Kenya's Indian Ocean coastline. The site covers about 390 acres of forest.
The prospect of mining in the area has raised concerns among local residents, who fear the project could damage the forest and threaten their ancestral heritage.
There are also questions over whether communities living near the site will benefit from the investment.

Barnett was keen to reassure Kenyans that they would benefit: "We intend to create lasting opportunities for Kenyan workers, businesses and the wider economy through capacity-building and targeted investment, while prioritising environmental management and performance."
The consortium must still obtain a prospecting licence and meet the necessary regulatory requirements before the project can proceed.
The tender decision has drawn objections from competing bidders.
Reuters news agency reports that two rival companies intend to challenge the selection, with Australia's RareX alleging that Frontier Minerals missed an earlier submission deadline.
Kenya's government has maintained that the process was open and transparent.
The project comes as US strives to secure alternative sources of critical minerals and reduce dependence on China, which dominates the processing of several key minerals.

Washington has been pursuing partnerships with mineral-rich African countries, including the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia, as it seeks to strengthen supply chains for industries ranging from electric vehicles to defence technology.
Kenya's mining ministry says the sector is an important part of its plans to diversify the economy beyond traditional sources of revenue such as tourism, agriculture and financial services.

content: President William Ruto has commenced his 10-day development tour of Western Kenya, with visits to Busia, Kakamega, Vihiga and Bungoma counties as his administration seeks to strengthen its presence in the region ahead of the 2027 General Election.
The tour follows a week-long visit to the region in March and comes after Ruto met Western Kenya leaders on Tuesday, November 17, to review ongoing projects and discuss new development priorities.

The meeting, led by National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula, brought together governors, MPs and senior government officials from the four counties. Discussions focused on healthcare, road infrastructure, affordable housing, industrial development and education.
Ruto highlighted reforms in the sugar sector, saying the revival of struggling public factories had improved farmers’ earnings and ensured workers received regular salaries.

Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi and Wetang’ula have been at the forefront of efforts to rally political support for Ruto in Western Kenya, where other regional leaders have aligned themselves with the opposition.
Mudavadi said the government remained committed to ensuring Western Kenya benefits from national development programmes and that all communities are included in the country’s development agenda.

items.title: Ruto Rejects Politics of Exclusion, Pledges Equal Development
Ruto roots for equitable development as he tours Western Kenya
items.description: All parts of Kenya have an equal right to development, President William Ruto has said. The President called out leaders advocating the politics of exclusion on account of a community’s voting numbers or population.- Advertisement - He said no part of the country and no community would be left out in the country’s ambitious transformation […]
content: All parts of Kenya have an equal right to development, President William Ruto has said.
The President called out leaders advocating the politics of exclusion on account of a community’s voting numbers or population.
He said no part of the country and no community would be left out in the country’s ambitious transformation agenda, adding that all Kenyans would be treated equally.
“Do you want to be told about shares? Do you want to be told you come from a small community or you are few?” he asked.
He was speaking on the first day of his development tour of Western Kenya when he opened Kakapel Iteso Cultural Centre in Teso North Constituency, Busia County.
The cultural centre is dedicated to preserving and promoting the rich heritage of the Iteso community.
The President announced that the Government would allocate additional funds to expand and enhance the facility’s capacity to attract visitors from Kenya and beyond.
He was accompanied by Prime Cabinet Secretary Musallia Mudavadi, National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetangula, Busia Governor Paul Otuoma and MPs, among others.
The President said he is committed to uniting the country and eradicating the politics of discrimination, hatred and tribalism.
He explained that this is why he joined forces with the Orange Democratic Movement and other parties to form the Broad-Based Government.
“We want every Kenyan to feel like they belong in Kenya and enjoy equal rights,” he said.
President Ruto urged Kenyans to carefully vet leaders seeking elective positions and elect those with a track record and agenda, pointing out that the opposition has no vision for Kenya.
Earlier, the President also laid a foundation stone for the Akichelesit General Service Unit (GSU) Camp in Teso North Constituency, which will strengthen security in the region.
He also said the Government will invest KSh100 million in housing for police officers deployed to the camp, providing them with decent living conditions as they serve and protect the people.

The Government is committed, he explained, to providing adequate housing and equipment to enable security officers to fully execute their constitutional mandate of protecting the lives and property of Kenyans.
Mr Mudavadi said President Ruto is keen on building the necessary infrastructure in the Western region to ensure trade with Uganda prospers.
He said the President stands for the politics of equality, ensuring no region is left behind.
“Let us, therefore, as a community and as a region, join forces with President Ruto to secure victory in 2027,” he said.
Speaker Wetangula noted that the Malaba-Mombasa road is a crucial transport corridor in Kenya but had been neglected.
He noted that the President will soon be unveiling the construction of a dual carriageway from Mombasa to reduce congestion, and boost business and livelihoods.
Governor Otuoma said Busia County had been left behind for a long time, but pointed out that under the leadership of President Ruto, the county’s transformation is on course.
“After 10 years of President Ruto, you will not recognise Busia County,” he said.
Mr Oparanya noted that the President is delivering on his commitments, citing the Malaba Smart City which, he said, would set the county on the path to transformation.

Edwin Sifuna Breaks Silence on Babu Owino Fallout, Defends How He Became Linda Mwananchi Party Leader
items.description: Edwin Sifuna explains how he became Linda Mwananchi party leader, challenging Babu Owino's claims that an earlier leadership agreement was changed.
content: Edwin Sifuna explains how he became Linda Mwananchi party leader, challenging Babu Owino's claims that an earlier leadership agreement was changed.

Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna has broken his silence on the growing leadership tensions within the Linda Mwananchi movement, revealing how he emerged as party leader and presidential candidate despite an earlier political arrangement that allegedly favoured Embakasi East MP Babu Owino.

In an interview with Citizen Radio, Sifuna rejected accusations that he had betrayed his political allies, insisting that the decision to appoint him was reached collectively after months of negotiations involving leaders seeking a common political vehicle.
His explanation comes after Babu publicly claimed that the original agreement was for Sifuna to become the movement's presidential candidate while he assumed the position of party leader.
The Embakasi East MP alleged that the arrangement subsequently changed without his knowledge, with some members insisting that whoever sought the presidency should also control the party.

However, Sifuna has now offered a different account, shifting attention to the negotiations that preceded the formation of their political outfit and the disagreements that emerged over party ownership and leadership.

The dispute threatens to expose deeper divisions within a movement that has increasingly positioned itself as an alternative political force following disagreements with the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM).
According to Sifuna , the disagreements started after the leaders were pushed out of ODM and began searching for a political vehicle through which they could pursue their ambitions.
He said the initial understanding was that members would abandon their individual political parties and consolidate their interests under one organisation.
The Nairobi Senator described the arrangement as an attempt to establish a common political home capable of accommodating all the leaders.
He disclosed that five politicians presented their existing political parties for consideration. They included Babu Owino, Caroli Omondi, Godfrey Osotsi, George Natembeya and Caleb Amisi.
The group subsequently established a subcommittee comprising the owners of the respective political parties.
Its responsibility was to submit party registration documents to lawyers for an assessment of their structures, ownership, registration status and legal compliance.
After evaluating the available options, Sifuna said the leaders agreed to settle on the Equitable Party as their common political vehicle.
He cited Caroli Omondi as one of the politicians who abandoned his own party to join the arrangement.
Former Meru Governor Kawira Mwangaza and Mavoko MP Patrick Makau also joined the political arrangement.

The Senator's account suggests that the initial negotiations were not simply about deciding who would occupy senior positions but also about identifying a legally suitable organisation that could accommodate the movement's political ambitions.
The dispute gained momentum after Babu claimed that he had initially agreed to allow Sifuna to become the movement's presidential candidate while he took charge of the party.
According to the Embakasi East MP, that understanding was later altered when some members argued that the presidential candidate should automatically become party leader.
The change reportedly caught him by surprise, raising questions about whether the movement's senior politicians had honoured their original political agreements.
However, Sifuna challenged the suggestion that he had manipulated the negotiations or deliberately sidelined Babu.
He maintained that the leadership structure was agreed upon collectively after the group settled on the Equitable Party.

Addressing the controversy, Sifuna defended his appointment as both party leader and presidential candidate, questioning the logic of trusting him with the country's highest office while denying him control of the political outfit.
“Is it possible you trust me to be president of the country but you cannot trust me to be party leader of a party?” he posed.
The Senator insisted that his colleagues had participated in the discussions and that the decision was not an individual undertaking.
He also rejected suggestions that the arrangement was designed to diminish Babu's political influence within the movement.
However, Sifuna acknowledged that some leaders later reconsidered their positions after recognising the political advantages of retaining control of their individual parties.
He said the group accepted their decision and allowed them to continue leading their respective political outfits.
“So we agreed. If you must be party leader so people enter your party, it's okay. You can be party leader,” he explained.
The remarks expose a fundamental disagreement within Linda Mwananchi over whether political unity should take precedence over individual control of party structures.

For politicians preparing for the 2027 General Election, party ownership carries significant strategic importance, particularly when negotiating nominations, controlling grassroots networks and determining who occupies influential positions.
Despite the public disagreements, Sifuna dismissed reports suggesting that his relationship with Babu, Siaya Governor James Orengo, Godfrey Osotsi and other members of the movement had collapsed.
He maintained that none of the leaders had personally confronted him over allegations of betrayal.
“When you talk about rumours, especially these rumours I see on social media, Babu himself or Orengo or Caleb hasn't said that Sifuna has wronged him anywhere,” he said.
The Senator challenged commentators to distinguish between disagreements over political arrangements and a complete breakdown in personal relationships.
He also urged his colleagues to concentrate on building the political movement rather than allowing leadership disagreements to dominate its public image.
“The hope that Kenyans have placed in Linda Mwananchi does not allow me to have side shows,” he said.
Sifuna further disclosed that the group had conducted more than 100 meetings in an effort to persuade its members to consolidate their political interests under one party.
His remarks suggest that the negotiations have been considerably more complicated than the public disagreements indicate.
However, the competing accounts from Sifuna and Babu leave unanswered questions about the precise terms of their original agreement and how the final leadership arrangement was reached.
With the 2027 elections approaching, the movement faces a difficult test of whether its leading politicians can reconcile their individual ambitions and establish a unified political structure.
The bigger question is whether Linda Mwananchi can survive the struggle for party control long enough to become a credible national political force.

Nyeri Catholic Archbishop threatens to sack officials who let politicians into the pulpit
items.description: Nyeri Catholic Archbishop Anthony Muheria has threatened to dismiss priests, catechists, coordinators and church secretaries who allow politicians to address congregations, issuing one of the starkest warnings yet from Kenya's Catholic leadership as political pressure on places of worship intensifies ahead of the 10 August 2027 General Election.
content: between church and state, warning that any official who hands a politician a microphone will be dismissed immediately

Nyeri Catholic Archbishop Anthony Muheria has threatened to dismiss priests, catechists, coordinators and church secretaries who allow politicians to address congregations, issuing one of the starkest warnings yet from Kenya’s Catholic leadership as political pressure on places of worship intensifies ahead of the 10 August 2027 General Election.

Muheria delivered the directive as the Catholic Church escalates its campaign to keep politicians from converting Sunday services into campaign rallies — a practice that reached uncomfortable levels during the 2022 election cycle and shows every sign of repeating itself as Kenya enters another charged electoral season. With barely eight months to polling day, the pews have become some of the most coveted real estate in Kenyan politics, offering candidates direct access to organised, attentive and community-rooted audiences that no roadside rally can replicate.

The Archbishop was unambiguous about the consequences for those who facilitate such access. “Whoever allows a leader — anyone among you who allows anybody to speak in the church — will be fired immediately,” he declared. He extended the warning explicitly to administrative staff, making clear that arranging an opportunity for a politician to address worshippers was itself a dismissible offence. “If you are a coordinator, a secretary, and you are the one who arranged this thing, know that once it reaches me, you have lost your job and we will have an election to get another secretary,” he said.

The language was deliberate and pointed — the word “election” applied not to the national contest for public office but to the internal process of replacing a church official who had compromised the sanctity of the institution. It was a sharp piece of rhetorical symmetry, and it conveyed Muheria’s message with unmistakable clarity: the Church will govern itself by its own standards, regardless of the political weather outside its doors.

His frustration with the 2022 experience was evident. That election period saw politicians engage in heated and at times undignified confrontations inside churches, with congregations pressed into service as audiences for attacks on opponents and displays of political rivalry. Muheria cited those scenes as precisely what the current directive is designed to prevent. “Let us keep politics out of here, so that we can have respect in our churches,” he said.

He went further, drawing a sharp and deliberately colourful line between the spaces he considers appropriate for political contest and those he does not. “Let them go to bars, those dens. Let them go there into the fields — there is where they can fight, let them pull each other in the mud. But the church is God’s,” Muheria stated. The image was vivid and intentional: politics, in his framing, belongs to the rough and contested public square, not to the consecrated space where communities gather in a different spirit entirely.

Muheria’s directive follows a formal position adopted by the Kenya Conference of Catholic Bishops, which has barred politicians from delivering political addresses in churches across the country. The bishops argued that politicians have no shortage of alternative platforms — television, radio, public barazas, roadside rallies — through which to advance their agendas and seek support. What they do not have, the bishops maintained, is a right to the church’s platform, its congregation or its moral authority.

That authority is precisely what makes churches so attractive to Kenyan politicians. In a country where community trust in formal institutions has been eroded by years of broken promises and governance failures, the church retains a credibility that political parties and government agencies have largely forfeited. A politician who can stand before a congregation — or better still, be seen to receive the implicit endorsement of a priest or bishop — gains something that money and advertising cannot easily manufacture. The Catholic Church’s directive is, at its core, a refusal to allow that credibility to be borrowed for electoral purposes.

The timing carries additional significance. Kenya’s political landscape is shifting rapidly as the 2027 election approaches. Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua is consolidating opposition in the Mt Kenya region through his Democracy for the Citizens Party. The Linda Mwananchi Movement is expanding its national footprint. President William Ruto is defending his record against a cost-of-living narrative that has tested public patience. In that environment, every platform matters — and the Catholic Church, with its reach into rural and urban communities across the country, represents one of the most significant platforms of all.

By drawing its boundary now, eight months before polling day, the Church is sending a message that it intends to be a moral voice in the 2027 election rather than a political prop. Whether that boundary holds as campaign pressure mounts will be one of the quieter but consequential tests of institutional integrity in the months ahead.
The church, Muheria has made clear, is God’s. The mud is available elsewhere.

items.title: Ruto’s State of the Nation: Billions promised
items.description: President William Ruto delivered his fourth State of the Nation Address to Parliament on Wednesday, announcing the settlement of KSh 61.8 billion in long-outstanding government obligations, pledging police accountability reforms and issuing a pointed, if unnamed, rebuke of former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua's campaign to consolidate the Mt Kenya region behind his Democracy for the Citizens Party ahead of the 10 August 2027 General Election.
content: President William Ruto used his fourth address to Parliament to announce KSh 61.8B in debt settlements, healthcare gains and a major northern road — while firing an unmistakable political shot at Rigathi Gachagua ahead of 2027

President William Ruto delivered his fourth State of the Nation Address to Parliament on Wednesday, announcing the settlement of KSh 61.8 billion in long-outstanding government obligations, pledging police accountability reforms and issuing a pointed, if unnamed, rebuke of former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua’s campaign to consolidate the Mt Kenya region behind his Democracy for the Citizens Party ahead of the 10 August 2027 General Election.

The address, delivered to a joint sitting of the National Assembly and the Senate in Nairobi, covered ground ranging from university and hospital debts to highway expansion, healthcare registration and examination integrity — but it was the political undercurrent that gave the speech its sharpest edge. With Kenya’s electoral clock ticking toward August 2027, Ruto used the constitutional platform of Parliament to frame the coming contest on his terms: a debate about policy, delivery and evidence, not personality and regional loyalty.

“No community should be reduced to a voting bloc. No region should be asked to surrender its judgement to a personality,” he told lawmakers, in remarks whose target, while unnamed, was unmistakable. Gachagua has spent recent weeks describing Mt Kenya as DCP territory, warning residents against incumbent legislators allied to the ruling United Democratic Alliance and declaring a political “transfer window” open until 31 December. On Tuesday, one day before Ruto’s address, Gachagua received three sitting MPs at his Wamunyoro residence — Gatundu South’s Gabriel Kagombe, Nyeri Woman Representative Rahab Mukami and Laikipia West’s Wachira Karani — and declared DCP “the party of the moment and the future.”

Ruto’s response was measured but deliberate. He called on all political actors — beginning with his own administration — to submit to a standard of evidence-based accountability. “Those who offer alternatives must explain their proposals. All of us must respect the people’s right to question, scrutinise and choose,” he said, challenging rivals to articulate how they would lower electricity costs, finance infrastructure, expand employment and improve healthcare. It was a calculated pivot: shifting the 2027 conversation from the grievance politics that Gachagua has cultivated toward a terrain where an incumbent with a delivery record believes he holds the advantage.

On financial settlements, Ruto announced the approval of KSh 18 billion owed to public and private universities and KSh 16 billion owed to hospitals under the now-defunct National Hospital Insurance Fund. Both payments, he said, were undergoing processing at the National Treasury and would be disbursed within weeks. He also announced the settlement of 28,726 verified pending bills amounting to KSh 27.8 billion, covering claims dating back to 2005. “These payments are undergoing the due process at the National Treasury for payment in the coming weeks,” he said, arguing that the disbursements would restore cash flow to businesses, protect jobs and ease financial pressure across multiple sectors.

In education, the President cited the recruitment of 100,000 teachers over four years against a shortage of 116,000 when his administration assumed office, with a further 20,000 to be recruited. He said the government had constructed 23,000 classrooms, was equipping 1,600 laboratories and had increased the annual education budget from KSh 521 billion in 2022/23 to KSh 784 billion currently. Notably, he revealed that for the first time in 65 years, Kenya’s national examination papers had been printed locally — a quiet but symbolically significant assertion of institutional capacity. Some 3.6 million candidates were sitting the KPSEA, KJSEA and KCSE examinations, he added, in conditions described as calm and orderly.

Healthcare figures dominated a significant portion of the address. Ruto said 33.7 million Kenyans had registered with the Social Health Authority, compared to approximately eight million under NHIF in 2022. He cited 53,465 patients receiving cancer treatment, 24,468 undergoing dialysis and 89 who had received kidney transplants under the scheme. “Through SHA, cover treatment costs are being financed on behalf of citizens, reducing the amounts that families would otherwise have to raise from either their savings, borrow from relatives, or obtain through sale of their assets,” he said. He acknowledged the troubled transition from NHIF to SHA but maintained that the long-term objective remained the progressive removal of catastrophic medical expenses from household budgets.

On infrastructure, Ruto confirmed that plans to dual the Nairobi–Mombasa Highway — approximately 460 kilometres — had reached an advanced stage, with the Kenya National Highways Authority estimating costs at around KSh 300 billion. He said the project would proceed without new taxes or additional public debt, though the proposed toll-road model has drawn scrutiny from the Motorists Association of Kenya, which has called for full public disclosure of the financing structure. Ruto also announced the Northern Kenya Gateway Corridor, a 750-kilometre road linking Isiolo, Wajir and Mandera — a project he acknowledged had attracted widespread mockery when first proposed. “Some have lived their entire lives without a single tarmacked road reaching their communities. Their entire lives,” he said, invoking the equity imperative that has become a recurring theme of his administration.

The most consequential passage of the address, however, may prove to be his remarks on police accountability — a subject that has shadowed his presidency since the June 2024 anti-Finance Bill protests. The Independent Policing Oversight Authority has documented 127 deaths across three major protest periods, while Missing Voices recorded 24 police-related killings in May 2026 alone. Ruto acknowledged the pain of those events, confirmed a KSh 2 billion compensation allocation and said KSh 1.2 billion had already been paid to 1,476 verified beneficiaries. He was unequivocal that compensation did not replace criminal accountability. “Investigations must continue, and prosecutions must follow for violations of the law, wherever the evidence warrants,” he said.

His pledge to strengthen de-escalation procedures, oversight mechanisms and professional standards within the police service will be measured against a record that rights organisations have consistently found wanting. IPOA has cited forensic bottlenecks and evidentiary challenges; by June 2026, only three cases had reached the courts.

As State of the Nation addresses go, Wednesday’s was dense with numbers, ambitious in scope and strategically timed. With barely eight months to the 10 August 2027 election, every figure announced, every road promised and every political line drawn carries a dual purpose — governance and campaign. Ruto knows it. So does Gachagua.
The question Kenya will spend the next eight months answering is which of them is right.

Saudi Arabia Travel Ban on Kenyans Holds Even as UAE Reopens Doors to Ugandans
items.description: Saudi Arabia maintains its Kenya visa ban despite no new Ebola cases, while the UAE reopens to Ugandans after 21 days, leaving Kenyan workers still stranded.
content: PAY ATTENTION: Mark TUKO.co.ke as a preferred source, and our content will appear higher in your Google feed!

Saudi Arabia is holding firm on its travel and visa suspension against Kenya even as the United Arab Emirates has begun reopening its doors to travellers from Uganda , exposing a sharp divide in how Gulf nations are responding to the Ebola outbreak that swept through East Africa.

The Saudi restrictions, which took effect on October 30, 2026, bar Saudi nationals from travelling to Kenya and block entry to anyone who has been in Kenya or any other Ebola-affected country within the 21 days before arriving in the kingdom.
US issues travel warning against top destination for thousands of Kenyan workers in Gulf
The measures apply regardless of whether a traveller transits through a third country.

Saudi authorities tied the restrictions to their own national health assessments, triggered after Kenya confirmed an imported Ebola case on October 6, 2026, involving a traveller who had entered from the Democratic Republic of the Congo via Uganda.

Kenya's last confirmed case was recorded on October 19, and the final patient was discharged on November 11, 2026. A 42-day countdown to an official Ebola-free declaration began on November 12 and is due to conclude on December 23, 2026, if no new cases arise.
Kenya's Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale has described the Saudi measures as "excessive" and "not backed by the current epidemiological situation".
The Foreign Ministry has characterised them as a "blanket, punitive measure" unsupported by evidence. Diplomatic talks with Riyadh are ongoing, but no shift in Saudi policy has been announced.

The UAE had imposed a comparable suspension in June 2026 covering Uganda, the DRC and South Sudan. On November 11, 2026, its National Emergency, Crisis and Disasters Management Authority, acting in coordination with health and identity authorities, lifted the restriction for Uganda alone .
UAE lifts visa ban on East African country, imposes strict 21-day entry condition
Ugandan nationals can now apply for UAE visas and gain entry provided at least 21 days have passed since leaving Uganda.
Students, embassy staff and diplomatic passport holders are exempt from the waiting period, while restrictions on the DRC and South Sudan remain active.
Uganda's Foreign Affairs Minister, Ambassador Adonia Ayebare, publicly thanked the UAE government for reconsidering the restrictions.
The continued Saudi ban carries real consequences.
More than 300 Kenyans who travelled to Saudi Arabia in search of work were turned back at entry points in early November.

The kingdom has long been a major destination for Kenyan domestic workers, healthcare professionals, drivers and construction labourers, and remittances from Saudi Arabia were already under strain in 2026.
The situation differs markedly with the UAE, which has not imposed a blanket ban on Kenyan nationals.
The Emirates recently extended its visa-on-arrival programme to include eligible Kenyans, keeping that corridor open.
Kenya's diplomatic path forward rests significantly on the countdown to the December 23 Ebola-free declaration, which would give Nairobi a firmer basis to press Riyadh for a formal review.
Saudi Arabia has not signalled, however, that a Kenyan declaration would automatically result in the lifting of its restrictions.

items.description: Kenya Revenue Authority’s reverse invoicing lets factories issue eTIMS invoices for farmers, with consent, SMS alerts and buyer-paid costs easing compliance.
content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.

The Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) unveiled a reverse invoicing arrangement under which factories and other agricultural produce buyers can generate electronic tax invoices on behalf of small-scale farmers, removing the need for individual farmers to operate their own invoicing systems.
KRA Commissioner for Micro and Small Taxpayers George Obell announced the arrangement at the KRA Citizen Assembly, a taxpayer town hall held at Murang'a University on Tuesday, November 17, 2026.

Obell said the arrangement addresses a persistent challenge in agricultural supply chains where large processors deal with numerous smallholder suppliers who may lack the equipment, internet connectivity, or technical know-how to issue eTIMS invoices independently.
KRA issues November 20 deadline for 5 key taxes: Here’s what you need to know
Under the arrangement, an approved buyer such as a dairy processor documents the transaction directly within eTIMS, capturing details including the quantity of produce received and the agreed price.

A dairy factory buying milk from smallholder farmers, for instance, can generate an invoice reflecting each delivery without requiring each farmer to maintain a separate invoicing system.
This benefits buyers as well, since the generated invoices serve as valid documentation to support expense claims when filing tax returns.
Before any buyer can use the system, KRA requires them to complete a Know Your Customer process and obtain explicit approval from the authority.
Farmers must give informed consent before invoices can be raised in their name, and they receive notifications by SMS or email each time a transaction is recorded.
Inua Jamii registration 2026: Who qualifies, requirements and how to apply
Farmers can also independently monitor and validate invoices through their eTIMS dashboard.
Buyers are required to capture the farmer's KRA PIN, the quantity supplied, and the transaction price, and must maintain a full audit trail of all records.
KRA also stipulates that buyers must absorb the operational costs of the reverse invoicing functionality rather than passing them on to farmers.
The arrangement is not entirely new. KRA introduced reverse invoicing on December 27, 2024, initially capturing transactions worth KSh 800 million.
At that point, approximately 800 buyers had used the system to generate around 4,500 invoices for small suppliers.

The renewed push comes after KRA issued a public notice on November 10, 2025, confirming that from January 1, 2026, declared income and expenses in tax returns would be validated against eTIMS records.
That requirement exposed a documentation gap for businesses buying produce from farmers unable to issue compliant electronic invoices.

Reverse invoicing is positioned as one of several solutions, alongside eTIMS Lite services accessible through eCitizen and USSD, designed to draw informal and small-scale suppliers into the electronic tax framework.
Obell encouraged farmers encountering difficulties with the process to contact KRA offices or reach out through the authority's official communication channels for assistance.

items.title: Fund chips: Zimbabwean billionaire hunts for KSh 129b to invest in Kenya, Africa
items.description: Zimbabwean billionaire Strive Masiyiwa's Cassava Technologies is courting US and Middle East investors for up to $1bn (KSh129bn) to buy Nvidia chips.
content: PAY ATTENTION: Mark TUKO.co.ke as a preferred source, and our content will appear higher in your Google feed!

Elijah Ntongai is an experienced editor at TUKO.co.ke, with more than four years in financial, business, labour and technology research and reporting. His work provides valuable insights into Kenyan, African, and global trends.

Cassava Technologies, the pan-African digital infrastructure company founded by Zimbabwean billionaire Strive Masiyiwa, is in private discussions with potential investors in the United States and the Middle East to raise up to KSh 129 billion (USD 1 billion).

As reported first by Bloomberg, the capital is intended to fund the purchase of Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs), the semiconductors that power modern AI systems, and to strengthen the company's fibre-optic and data centre networks to meet rising demand for AI computing across Africa.
TikTok, ICC launch commerce labs to train Kenyan small businesses with growth skills

Should the raise succeed, it would add to an already substantial investment drive at Cassava. The company has committed to deploying 12,000 Nvidia chips across planned AI facilities in South Africa , Egypt, Kenya, and Nigeria as part of a wider KSh 93 billion (USD 720 million) programme to establish five AI computing hubs on the continent.

A facility in Cape Town is already operational, with additional locations planned in Johannesburg, Egypt, Kenya, Morocco, and Nigeria .

Separately, Cassava is partnering with Vodafone Business and Egyptian industrial group Elsewedy Electric on a KSh 129 billion (USD 1 billion) data centre development in Egypt, which will include the country's first sovereign AI data centre.
The project is expected to begin with 20 megawatts of capacity and scale to 200 megawatts over time, potentially creating around 200 direct jobs and 2,000 indirect ones.

Cassava holds the distinction of being Nvidia's first cloud partner based in Africa. Both Google and Nvidia are among its existing shareholders, connecting the company to two of the most influential players in global AI.
Elon Musk's Starlink banned from operating in top African country
Masiyiwa, born in 1961, built his business empire through Econet Wireless after a prolonged legal fight to obtain a mobile operating licence in Zimbabwe.

Cassava Technologies was later established as a separate pan-African platform encompassing Liquid Intelligent Technologies, which operates more than 116,000 kilometres of fibre-optic network, and Africa Data Centres. Forbes estimates his net worth at $2.2 billion as of 2026.

The KSh 129 billion (USD 1 billion) figure represents a fundraising target, not money already secured, and the discussions may not result in a completed deal. If finalised, it would rank among the largest private capital raises for digital infrastructure in African history.
The fundraising effort comes as Nvidia navigates a period of internal turbulence.
Co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as president and chief executive on November 12, 2026, following revelations of a personal scandal.

CFO Colette Kress has assumed the role of interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement. More than 158,000 people, including over 7,500 self-identified Nvidia employees, signed an open letter calling for Huang's reinstatement by November 15, with Elon Musk among those publicly backing the campaign.
Payaza enters Kenya’s digital payments market after securing CBK licence
Nvidia has stated that its operations, customer commitments, and product roadmap will continue uninterrupted.
No African partner, including Cassava, has announced any project delays linked to the leadership transition.

Platforms such as TikTok have changed how consumers discover products, interact with brands and make purchasing decisions. For many small businesses, a compelling […]
content: From fashion and handmade crafts to interior design and lifestyle content, Kenyan entrepreneurs are increasingly using social media to turn creative ideas into businesses, tapping into audiences that extend beyond traditional marketplaces.

Platforms such as TikTok have changed how consumers discover products, interact with brands and make purchasing decisions. For many small businesses, a compelling video or a well-told brand story can now be as important as having a physical shop.

This shift was among the issues explored at a Nairobi gathering on Wednesday, November 18, organised by TikTok and the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) as they launched the Digital Commerce Labs, an initiative intended to equip small businesses across Sub-Saharan Africa with digital commerce skills.
TikTok’s Head of Global Institution Engagement, Kushal Prakash, said the initiative was intended to help entrepreneurs benefit from the changing digital marketplace.

“We have seen how TikTok makes it easier for businesses to be discovered and influence purchase decisions through trends such as #TikTokMadeMeBuyIt. Social commerce has the power to unlock opportunities, level the playing field and equip Kenyan entrepreneurs with the tools to grow.”

In attendance to share their stories were content creators Cherie Kihato, founder of Savannah Space and a TikTok 2026 Global Discover List creator; Alix, founder of Mammacita in Pink; and Emmy Rono, Executive Director of Urembo Craft who shared their experiences of using digital content to communicate their brands, showcase their offerings and connect with potential customers.

Using their experiences, the forum aimed to showcase the wider change in how businesses approach marketing. Beyond advertising products, entrepreneurs are increasingly required to create content that tells stories, builds communities and gives audiences a reason to engage with their brands.

Dr Caroline Kaua, Director of Business Development, Marketing and Trade at the Micro and Small Enterprises Authority, said businesses needed the skills to adapt as digital platforms changed how consumers discovered and purchased products.

“Micro, small and medium enterprises play an important role in Kenya’s economy, creating jobs, supporting livelihoods and driving entrepreneurship,” she said. “As digital transformation continues to change how consumers discover and purchase products, it is important that our MSMEs have the skills and tools to adapt and take advantage of these changes.” According to a GSMA survey, 49 per cent of Kenyan businesses sell online exclusively through social media, while another 13 per cent combine social platforms with a website or online marketplace.
More than 40 per cent of internet users in Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa have also purchased products through social commerce platforms.

However, converting online attention into sustainable business growth requires more than simply posting regularly. Entrepreneurs need to understand their audiences, develop engaging content and identify ways to turn digital interactions into sales.

The programme will offer online learning modules and virtual, trainer-led sessions covering digital presence, content creation, artificial intelligence-driven e-commerce tools and strategies for reaching domestic and international markets.
ICC Deputy Secretary General Julian Kassum said digital commerce could create new opportunities for entrepreneurship, trade and job creation.

“Digital commerce is a powerful engine for inclusive growth. By equipping small businesses with the tools and skills they need to participate in the digital economy, we are opening new pathways for entrepreneurship, trade and job creation.”

items.description: Kenya’s 2027 Budget Policy Statement lists highways for private tolling, led by Nairobi–Thika’s KSh 100bn deal, amid legal hurdles after a High Court ruling.

Kenya's National Treasury has placed road tolling at the heart of its infrastructure financing strategy, releasing a pipeline of highway projects worth hundreds of billions of shillings that would transfer construction and maintenance costs from the government to private investors and motorists.

The proposals are contained in the 2027 Budget Policy Statement (BPS) and represent the government's most decisive shift yet towards a user-pay funding model for the country's busiest transport corridors, at a time when public debt servicing alone is projected to reach KSh 1.918 trillion in the 2027/28 financial year.

The most consequential project is the upgrade of the 461-kilometre Nairobi–Mombasa highway (A8), which the government intends to widen from two lanes to at least four and convert into an access-controlled toll road.
A previous proposal valued at KSh 468 billion, submitted by US investor Everstrong Capital, was rejected by the PPP Committee in July 2025 for failing to meet statutory requirements.
The revived plan has since moved to the transaction-adviser stage, with bid evaluation under way following a fresh expression of interest published in August 2026.
The Nairobi–Thika–Juja–Kenol–Sagana–Marua highway is listed as a KSh 100 billion PPP with a proposed 30-year concession period, targeting financial close in the 2028/29 financial year.

The Treasury has classified it as a user-pay investment without government support, meaning the private party absorbs all commercial and demand risk with no contingent liability falling on the Exchequer.
Isaya Yunge: How much Charlene Ruto's husband's Mercedes with custom plates costs

In western Kenya , the 243-kilometre Mau Summit–Eldoret–Malaba corridor, a section of the Northern Corridor carrying close to 3,000 trucks daily and over 35 million tonnes of cargo annually, is earmarked for upgrade to a four-lane toll road at an estimated KSh 130 billion, with construction pencilled in for June 2027 and financing expected from the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank.

Two bypass concessions round out the pipeline. The Nairobi Southern Bypass is set for a KSh 12.265 billion, 25-year operation and tolling concession, while the proposed 38.6-kilometre Mombasa Northern Bypass carries a KSh 30 billion price tag over 30 years, blending private capital with government viability-gap funding.

A High Court ruling in November 2026 has added complexity to the programme. The court declared portions of the PPP Act, 2021 unconstitutional insofar as they permit projects creating public debt or guarantees to bypass Parliament.

Pure user-pay toll roads without state backing can still proceed under committee approval, but any arrangement involving annuity payments or sovereign guarantees must now secure parliamentary consent.

The tolling agenda has also met organised resistance from consumer groups. The Motorists Association of Kenya (MAK) has rejected the proposed 30-year concession for the Rironi–Mau Summit highway , advocating instead for a temporary fuel levy of KSh 5 to KSh 10 per litre.
Kenyans have 4 days to submit views on Ruto's 2027/28 budget plan

The Consumer Federation of Kenya challenged a proposed KSh 8-per-kilometre toll on the Nairobi–Nakuru–Mau Summit corridor in court, arguing it would worsen the cost of living, though both petitions were dismissed.
None of the major projects has yet reached financial close, and toll rates remain undisclosed across the board.
With the Nairobi–Thika and bypass deals targeting 2028/29 for financial close, the entire programme will face continuity scrutiny in the period following Kenya's August 2027 General Election.

items.title: CBK backs Treasury bid to take control of county bank accounts
items.description: Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) Governor Kamau Thugge has backed a National Treasury proposal to move county governments’ funds into a single account at the Central Bank, saying the change would give the government a clearer view of public money and save taxpayers avoidable interest costs. Under amendments to the Public Finance Management (PFM) Act
content: Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) Governor Kamau Thugge has backed a National Treasury proposal to move county governments’ funds into a single account at the Central Bank, saying the change would give the government a clearer view of public money and save taxpayers avoidable interest costs.

Under amendments to the Public Finance Management (PFM) Act now before Parliament, the Treasury Single Account system, already used by the national government, would be extended to all 47 counties. Counties would need written approval from the National Treasury before opening or closing bank accounts, effectively shifting from multiple commercial bank accounts to a centralised system at the CBK.

Appearing before the Senate Standing Committee on Finance and Budget on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, Thugge said the reform would help the government track public funds and avoid borrowing when cash was already available.

“We fully support the amendments by ensuring county deposits are held at the Central Bank rather than across multiple commercial banks, the National Treasury gains better visibility and avoids incurring unnecessary interest payments when idle resources are already available,” he said.

The Treasury Single Account brings government bank accounts together under one structure, allowing public resources to be pooled and used efficiently. Under the system, ministries, departments and agencies transact through linked accounts within a consolidated Treasury structure, instead of maintaining separate stand-alone accounts in different banks.

Thugge, who helped draft the original PFM Act, said the change would also address the growing number of bank accounts held by county governments. He recommended limiting counties to one commercial bank imprest account, with their main operational and project accounts held at the CBK.
He said opening an account would generally require one-off approval, while county treasuries would retain control of their day-to-day finances.

CBK officials told the committee that 99 per cent of county transactions are already digital, adding that all 47 counties can open accounts and make payments remotely, including counties such as Wajir that have no CBK branch.
Senators on the committee, however, raised concerns about the proposal’s implications for county autonomy and service delivery.
Kakamega Senator Boni Khalwale questioned whether requiring Treasury approval for county bank accounts would interfere with the constitutional independence of the two levels of government.

“Management of public funds is a critical role of any government,” he said. “If the national government will now be involved in authorising bank accounts at the county level, does it not affect the constitutional provision that the two governments are independent?”

Committee Vice-Chairperson Tabitha Mutinda questioned whether the additional approval requirement would slow county operations. She cited existing delays in the release of funds through the Office of the Controller of Budget and raised concerns about semi-autonomous county entities, including municipalities, water companies and public hospitals, that manage Facility Improvement Funds.

Committee Chairperson Ali Roba urged the CBK to explore technological solutions to strengthen accountability. The committee plans to invite the National Treasury to present its position on the proposed amendments.
The Council of Governors has opposed the proposal, arguing that it would undermine the autonomy of county governments.

“We strongly oppose the proposal. It is against the letter and spirit of the Constitution that recognises counties as distinct governments with autonomy and not an appendage of the national government,” Council Chairperson Muthomi Njuki said.

He warned that the proposal would introduce another layer of approvals on top of clearances required from the Controller of Budget, potentially slowing the absorption of development funds and increasing pending bills.
Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka also criticised the proposal, saying it would undermine devolution.

The Kenya Urban Roads Authority (KURA) has announced a 10-day partial closure of a section of Gitanga Road in Kawangware, Nairobi, beginning Thursday, November 26, 2026.
According to a public notice issued by KURA, the affected stretch runs between kilometre 0+520 and kilometre 0+620.

The closure will remain in force from 6:00 AM on November 26 until 6:00 PM on December 5, 2026, to allow workers to safely construct a cross culvert intended to strengthen drainage capacity along the road.

KURA noted that although vehicular access through the section will be restricted, a pedestrian walkway will remain open throughout the construction period to ensure the continuous movement of foot traffic.

KURA has published a colour-coded diversion plan to guide motorists around the construction zone. Drivers heading into Kawangware are directed to use Naivasha Road, which connects to a diversion route leading back towards Gitanga Road.
Vehicles travelling towards Nairobi or seeking local access should take Salim Road, connecting through Macharia Road before rejoining Gitanga Road in the direction of the city centre.
Stricter conditions apply to public service vehicles and heavy goods vehicles weighing more than 7.5 tonnes.
These categories must use the Naivasha Road route to bypass the construction zone entirely and are not permitted to use the lighter diversion routes designated for private cars.
Traffic marshals and flagmen will be stationed at key intersections to assist with vehicle flow, and KURA is urging all motorists to follow the instructions of traffic police deployed at the site.

The authority has flagged that the affected section overlaps with a busy commercial zone near the Kawangware Open-Air Market and adjacent roadside traders, making extra vigilance necessary for road users passing through the area.

Apart from the Kawangware road, KURA also temporarily closed to Mlolongo-Kamulu Quarry Road and the alternative routes available to motorists.
The authority has also extended the Eldoret Road closure until 30 December, blaming construction delays linked to a Nairobi River bridge project.

items.description: Rachel Ruto opens SIBOH School and Sports Academy at Koilel Farm, blending Kenya’s competency-based curriculum with professional coaching in more than 15 sports.
content: PAY ATTENTION: Mark TUKO.co.ke as a preferred source, and our content will appear higher in your Google feed!
A new private institution combining academic learning with elite sports training has been officially opened on President William Ruto's Koilel Farm in Moiben, Uasin Gishu County .
First Lady Rachel Ruto presided over the launch of SIBOH School and Sports Academy Wednesday, November 18, at the campus along Naiberi Road.
The ceremony drew senior government officials including Basic Education Principal Secretary John Ololtuaa and Sports Principal Secretary Elijah Mwangi, alongside a number of political leaders.
Siboh School and Sports Academy: Inside William Ruto's modern academy
Speaking at the launch, the First Lady described the president as the driving force behind the project, recalling how the site looked before construction began.

She added that her husband saw something entirely different in that ground:

Rachel noted that SIBOH was conceived to "nurture dreams, discover talents, and prepare future generations for greatness," and that the school represents more than an investment in education and sports; it is an investment in the future of our children and our nation.
Rachel Ruto gives glimpse of new elite school and sports academy owned by William Ruto
The idea of the institution took shape in 2022, with the site selected in 2023 and construction and staff recruitment following in subsequent years.
SIBOH is an acronym for Servanthood, Integrity, Bravery, Optimism and Honour.

The Christian-based institution will teach under Kenya's Competency-Based Education framework across Pre-Primary, Primary, Junior School and Senior School levels, with the Senior School offering STEM, Social Sciences, and Arts and Sports Science pathways.

Drawing on Eldoret's status as a global distance-running hub, the academy will provide professional coaching in more than 15 disciplines, including athletics, football , rugby, swimming, basketball, volleyball, tennis, badminton, golf and cricket.

The campus features smart classrooms equipped with interactive touchscreen display boards, a purpose-built early-years hall with play structures and wooden shelving, a wellness centre staffed by qualified medical personnel, and boarding facilities operating a Farm-to-Fork catering approach.
The school also has safeguarding policies covering child protection, anti-bullying and digital safety.
Rachel revealed that the institution was in the process of hiring teachers and other staff.

The academy will admit its first learners in January 2027, with registration currently open.

Some sources indicate that termly tuition and meal fees range from KSh 90,000 at Pre-Primary level to KSh 370,000 depending on grade. Additional recurring charges include KSh 5,000 for medical cover and KSh 5,000 for enrichment programmes per term, while optional transport costs KSh 10,000 or KSh 15,000 return.
The school is led by Executive Director Victor Boiyo. Charlene Ruto was introduced at the launch as the institution's patron.
The corporate entity and shareholding structure behind SIBOH have not been publicly disclosed.

Glovo expands investment in Kenya with two new facilities, targets 1,000 additional riders by year-end
items.description: Glovo, a leading technology platform operating across Europe, Central Asia and Africa, has opened two new facilities in Nairobi as part of its KSh10 billion investment commitment in Kenya, reinforcing its focus on creating meaningful employment and income-generating opportunities for young Kenyans.
content: Glovo, a leading technology platform operating across Europe, Central Asia and Africa, has opened two new facilities in Nairobi as part of its KSh10 billion investment commitment in Kenya, reinforcing its focus on creating meaningful employment and income-generating opportunities for young Kenyans.

The new Real Time Operations (RTO) office and Glovo Centre mark another step in the company’s expansion in Kenya, following the opening of its regional office in Nairobi in May 2026, where Glovo announced plans to invest an additional KSh 10 billion in the country by 2030. The facilities are designed to strengthen Glovo’s operations while providing young people with opportunities to build careers, develop practical skills and improve their financial wellbeing.

The facilities were officially launched during a visit to Kenya by Glovo Co-founder, Sacha Michaud, who engaged with employees, riders and other stakeholders on the company’s growth plans and continued investment in the market.

Speaking during the launch, Michaud said, “When we announced our investment commitment earlier this year, our ambition was not simply to grow Glovo’s presence in Kenya, but to create more opportunities for people to earn, learn and build their futures. These new facilities are part of making that commitment a reality. We want young Kenyans working within our operations to have opportunities to develop their skills and grow their careers, while ensuring riders have access to the training and financial knowledge that can help them make the most of their earnings and pursue their own ambitions.”

The new Real Time Operations office reflects Kenya’s growing role as a hub for Glovo’s operations. Initially established to support six markets, the Nairobi-based department has significantly expanded its mandate and now provides round-the-clock operational support across 21 markets.

The expansion has also increased the office’s capacity from an initial 100 workstations to accommodate 220 staff members, with plans to significantly increase capacity further as operations grow. This investment is expected to create additional employment opportunities for young Kenyans, particularly those looking to build careers in technology-enabled operations and customer support.

Beyond employment, the RTO office provides an environment where young professionals can gain practical experience, develop operational and problem-solving skills, and build careers within Glovo’s wider business.
Alongside the RTO office, Glovo officially opened its first Glovo Centre in Kenya, a dedicated facility designed to bring rider onboarding, training, development and support services under one roof.

The Centre will provide riders with access to practical training and skills development opportunities, supporting them in managing their work on the platform while equipping them with knowledge that can be useful beyond deliveries, including in pursuing entrepreneurship and other income-generating opportunities.

To mark the opening, Glovo partnered with Centonomy to deliver a financial literacy training session for 50 riders, equipping them with practical financial management skills to help them better manage their earnings, develop a savings culture and plan for their financial futures.

The occasion also marked the launch of a rider-led Savings and Credit Cooperative Society (SACCO), established by Glovo riders themselves to encourage saving, improve access to credit and strengthen their financial wellbeing. Supported by Glovo, the initiative provides riders with an opportunity to collectively build financial security and access resources that can support their personal and entrepreneurial ambitions.

Through the new Glovo Centre, the company is targeting the onboarding of an additional 1,000 riders by the end of 2026, building on the 2,765 riders already onboarded in the first ten months of the year. The figure represents Glovo’s highest annual rider onboarding since entering the Kenyan market in 2019, reflecting its continued efforts to expand income-generating opportunities through the platform.

Since launching in Kenya in 2019, Glovo has grown to connect more than 6,000 businesses with customers through its platform, while over 12,400 riders have had the opportunity to earn income through deliveries.

The opening of the two facilities builds on Glovo’s long-term investment plans for Kenya, with a focus on expanding opportunities for young men and women to participate in the digital economy. Through employment, skills development, financial literacy and rider support initiatives, the company aims to ensure that its continued growth creates opportunities for people to build sustainable livelihoods and pursue their longer-term career and business ambitions.

Nairobi forum puts Africa’s voice at centre of global AI governance debate
items.description: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 19 – Scholars and legal practitioners from several countries have called for stronger international cooperation on artificial intelligence (AI) and data governance, warning that the rapid growth…
content: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 19 – Scholars and legal practitioners from several countries have called for stronger international cooperation on artificial intelligence (AI) and data governance, warning that the rapid growth of digital technologies risks deepening inequalities if countries and communities are excluded from shaping the rules.

The experts said fair digital governance must go beyond technological development to address data privacy, national sovereignty, accountability and equitable access to the benefits of the digital economy.

The concerns featured prominently at the inaugural Global Forum on Digital Intelligence, Rule of Law and Interdisciplinary Governance, hosted by the University of Nairobi’s Faculty of Law on November 17, bringing together participants from Kenya, China, South Africa, Japan, the United States and other countries.

Held under the theme “ Law, Innovation and China–Africa Cooperation in the Intelligent Age ,” the forum examined how countries can develop common approaches to regulating emerging technologies while protecting individual rights and ensuring that digital partnerships deliver shared benefits.

A key focus was the need to give African countries greater influence over the rules governing data and artificial intelligence, particularly as cross-border digital trade and the use of personal information expand.

items.title: Why did Kenya and Uganda see onward Ebola transmission while Nigeria had no secondary Cases?
items.description: Nigeria and Kenya have completed contact follow-up and are in the 42-day surveillance period. Uganda declared its outbreak over on 27 August.
content: Three countries imported Ebola from DR Congo in 2026, Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.
On 13 November, Nigeria completed 21 days of monitoring for all 62 contacts of its imported Bundibugyo Ebola case.
Thirteen developed symptoms and all tested negative.
The patient recovered after evacuation to Switzerland.
Remarkably, Nigeria detected zero secondary cases.
It seems there is good news across the region.
Nigeria and Kenya have completed contact follow-up and are in the 42-day surveillance period.
Uganda declared its outbreak over on 27 August.
Only the Democratic Republic of Congo is still reporting ongoing local transmission in this outbreak.
Kenya recorded nine confirmed cases and two deaths after one importation.
Four relatives and four health workers were infected.
All eight were already in quarantine when symptoms began, and no further spread was documented.
Uganda recorded 20 confirmed cases and two deaths, with 15 imported and five locally acquired infections​.
Nigeria itself had a different experience in 2014.
A traveller who arrived already ill with Zaire ebolavirus sparked an outbreak of 19 confirmed cases, one probable case and eight deaths.
Nine health workers acquired Ebola directly from him.
This time, the Abuja patient arrived from Uganda on 3 October and fell ill four days later.
She sought care on 10 October, was admitted the next day with fever and diarrhoea, and was initially treated for suspected malaria.
Ebola was confirmed on 20 October. She was potentially infectious during those nine days in hospital.
How many of her 62 contacts had direct, unprotected exposure to her body fluids, and what precautions were in place?
Historical Ebola household studies estimated secondary infection rates of 0.8 percent without direct contact and about 48 percent among people providing nursing care.
The difference matters because 62 listed contacts may include very few people with substantial exposure.
Her husband was among those followed, but we know little about the care he provided.
I wonder whether fewer people gave hands-on care in Abuja because of household routines or because she chose to limit contact while unwell.
The Kenyan patient died two days after admission and may have needed more intensive care.
Did more relatives spend time with him or provide hands-on care while he was ill?
The four occupational infections also warrant a review of the precautions used during initial care at The Nairobi Hospital.
A fair comparison requires exposure and infection-control records from both hospitals.
But people are yet to see a published account of who was exposed in Abuja before effective isolation.
The world would like to get a de-identified comparison of the Nigerian and Kenyan cases, with independent reporting on the findings.
Who provided care at home and in hospital? When did precautions begin?
What can available viral-load data tell us alongside the clinical timelines?
For now, the known chains of transmission in Kenya and Uganda have been contained, and Nigeria detected zero secondary cases.
Understanding how these different outcomes arose could help protect families and frontline staff from the first encounter, before anyone suspects Ebola.
